elements.context: πότερον μιμηταῖς τούτοις οὗτοι ἐντυχόντες ἐξηπάτηνται
εἰδώλου δημιουργός, ὃν δὴ μιμητὴν ὡρισάμεθα
πάντας τοὺς ποιητικοὺς μιμητὰς εἰδώλων ἀρετῆς εἶνααι
ὁ τοῦ εἰδώλου ποιητής, ὁ μιμητής
οὔτε ἄρα εἴσεται οὔτε ὀρθὰ δοξάσει ὁ μιμητὴς
χαρίεις ἂν εἴη ὁ ἐν τῇ ποιήσει μιμητικὸς
πάντας εἶναι μιμητικοὺς ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα

signals.observation: Forms of μιμητής and μιμητικός recur throughout the section, naming the imitator first as one who may have deceived listeners, then as the definition Homer has been placed under, then as the general category for all poets, and finally as the subject of accumulated negative conclusions about knowledge.

elements.context: τό τε μιμηθησόμενον καὶ τὸ εἴδωλον

signals.observation: εἴδωλον recurs in nominative, genitive, and accusative forms, naming what the imitator produces and is contrasted with τὸ μιμηθησόμενον and with ἀρετή.

elements.context: οὐκ αἰσθάνονται τριττὰ ἀπέχοντα τοῦ ὄντος
εἴπερ μὴ τρίτος ἀπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας εἶ ἀρετῆς πέρι

signals.observation: A spatial-numerical sequence is articulated: works of imitators are said to be three removes from τὸ ὄν, Homer is addressed as third from ἀλήθεια in relation to ἀρετή unless he is second, establishing a ranked distance from reality and truth.

elements.context: ἀλλʼ εἴπερ γε οἶμαι ἐπιστήμων εἴη τῇ ἀληθείᾳ
ἐὰν μὴ σφεῖς αὐτῶν ἐπιστατήσωσιν τῆς παιδείας
ὁ δὲ μιμητὴς πότερον ἐκ τοῦ χρῆσθαι ἐπιστήμην ἕξει

signals.observation: Forms of ἐπίσταμαι and ἐπιστήμη recur, first attributed to what some say the poets possess, then questioned regarding Homer, then assigned to the user of an object in the three-craft model, and finally denied to the imitator.

elements.context: τοῖς πολλοῖς τε καὶ μηδὲν εἰδόσιν

signals.observation: Forms of οἶδα recur, first attached to the requirement that a good poet must know, then to the user and maker in the three-craft model, and finally denied to the imitator who produces for those who do not know.

elements.context: εἰς τέχνας ἤ τινας ἄλλας πράξεις
περὶ ἕκαστον ταύτας τινὰς τρεῖς τέχνας εἶναι

signals.observation: τέχνη recurs, first as what poets are claimed to know all of, then as what the poet colors with words, then in the model of three crafts for each thing.

elements.context: περὶ ἕκαστον ταύτας τινὰς τρεῖς τέχνας εἶναι, χρησομένην, ποιήσουσαν, μιμησομένην

signals.observation: Three future participles in the feminine accusative singular are set in sequence to name three crafts: the one that will use, the one that will make, and the one that will imitate.
Forms of χράομαι recur in the articulation of the three-craft model, repeatedly naming the user as the one who has knowledge and instructs the maker.

elements.context: τίνας ὑγιεῖς ποιητής τις τῶν παλαιῶν ἢ τῶν νέων
τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἄρα σκεύους ὁ μὲν ποιητὴς πίστιν ὀρθὴν ἕξει

signals.observation: ποιητής recurs in different contexts: first as the good poet who must know, then as poets in general, then as the image-maker, and finally as the maker in the three-craft model who has correct belief but not knowledge.
ἀλήθεια recurs as what the imitator does not know, what Homer is third from, what one must be knowledgeable in, and finally what the poets do not touch.

elements.context: τούς τε τῆς τραγικῆς ποιήσεως ἁπτομένους

signals.observation: ἅπτω appears first negated with ἀλήθεια as the object poets do not touch, and returns with τραγική ποίησις as the object tragic poets do touch.

elements.context: ἰδίᾳ τισὶν ἡγεμὼν παιδείας αὐτὸς ζῶν λέγεται Ὅμηρος γενέσθαι
ὁ Κρεώφυλος...τοῦ ὀνόματος ἂν γελοιότερος ἔτι πρὸς παιδείαν φανείη

signals.observation: παιδεία recurs in questions about whether Homer was a leader in education, whether his companion would be laughable regarding it, and whether the sophists claim supervision of it is necessary.

elements.form: φαντάσματα γὰρ ἀλλʼ οὐκ ὄντα ποιοῦσιν
elements.context: φαντάσματα γὰρ ἀλλʼ οὐκ ὄντα ποιοῦσιν

signals.observation: imitators are said to make φαντάσματα but not ὄντα, contrasting appearances with beings.

elements.context: πολὺ πρότερον ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις ἂν σπουδάσειεν
πολλὰ καὶ καλὰ ἔργα ἑαυτοῦ καταλιπεῖν μνημεῖα

signals.observation: ἔργα is contrasted with μιμήματα: if one truly knew, one would care more for works than for imitations, and would leave many beautiful works as memorials.

elements.context: εἶναι προθυμοῖτʼ ἂν μᾶλλον ὁ ἐγκωμιαζόμενος

signals.observation: Participles of ἐγκωμιάζω are set in contrast: one would rather be the one praised than the one praising.

elements.context: μετὰ τοῦτο ἐπισκεπτέον τήν τε τραγῳδίαν καὶ τὸν ἡγεμόνα αὐτῆς Ὅμηρον

signals.observation: The opening states that tragedy and Homer must be examined; this is then reformulated as a question that must be investigated, and Glaucon affirms that it must be examined.

elements.context: Χαρώνδαν μὲν γὰρ Ἰταλία καὶ Σικελία

signals.observation: Three lawgivers are named—Lycurgus, Charondas, and Solon—each associated with cities or regions they benefited, establishing a pattern Homer is asked to match but cannot.

elements.context: ὥσπερ αὖ Θάλεώ τε πέρι τοῦ Μιλησίου

signals.observation: Thales and Anacharsis are named as examples of wise men whose practical inventions are remembered, a pattern Homer again fails to match.

elements.context: ὥσπερ Πυθαγόρας αὐτός τε διαφερόντως ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἠγαπήθη
καὶ οἱ ὕστεροι ἔτι καὶ νῦν Πυθαγόρειον τρόπον ἐπονομάζοντες τοῦ βίου

signals.observation: Pythagoras is named and his followers are described as still naming their way of life Pythagorean, providing a model of a teacher whose influence persisted through a named way of life.

elements.context: ὁ γὰρ Κρεώφυλος, ὦ Σώκρατες, ὁ τοῦ Ὁμήρου ἑταῖρος

signals.observation: Creophylus is named as Homer's companion and said to be even more laughable than his name regarding education, with the report that much neglect surrounded Homer while he lived.
Protagoras and Prodicus are named as sophists who convince people in private conversation that they cannot manage house or city without their supervision.

elements.context: Πυθαγόρας αὐτός τε διαφερόντως ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἠγαπήθη
καὶ ἐτιμᾶτο καὶ ἠγαπᾶτο ὑπʼ αὐτῶν

signals.observation: Forms of ἀγαπάω recur in describing how Pythagoras was loved for his teaching, how his followers loved him for association, and in the counterfactual question about whether Homer would have been loved if he could truly educate.

elements.context: Ὅμηρον...ἢ Ἡσίοδον ῥαψῳδεῖν ἂν περιιόντας εἴων

signals.observation: The activity of going around rhapsodizing is mentioned as what people would have allowed Homer and Hesiod to do if they could not truly benefit people toward virtue.

elements.context: αὐτός τε οὐκ ἐπαΐων περὶ σκυτοτομίας
ποιήσει δέ γε σκυτοτόμος καὶ χαλκεύς
οὐδʼ ὁ ποιήσας, ὅ τε χαλκεὺς καὶ ὁ σκυτεύς

signals.observation: Forms referring to shoemaking and shoemakers recur throughout the extended example of the three crafts, first illustrating what a painter can represent without knowledge, then used in the model of user, maker, and imitator.

elements.context: ἆρʼ οὖν ἐπαΐει οἵας δεῖ τὰς ἡνίας εἶναι καὶ τὸν χαλινὸν ὁ γραφεύς
ἐκ τοῦ χρῆσθαι ἐπιστήμην ἕξει περὶ ὧν ἂν γράφῃ
ζωγράφος, φαμέν, ἡνίας τε γράψει καὶ χαλινόν

signals.observation: References to the painter (ζωγράφος, γραφεύς) and painting (γράφω) recur as the consistent example of the imitator who lacks knowledge.

elements.context: οἵας δεῖ τὰς ἡνίας εἶναι καὶ τὸν χαλινόν
ἐκεῖνος ὅσπερ τούτοις ἐπίσταται χρῆσθαι, μόνος ὁ ἱππικός

signals.observation: Reins, bridle, and the horseman form a cluster of horse-related equipment and expertise used to illustrate the three-craft model.

elements.context: ποιήσει δέ γε σκυτοτόμος καὶ χαλκεύς
οὐδʼ ὁ ποιήσας, ὅ τε χαλκεὺς καὶ ὁ σκυτεύς

signals.observation: The bronzeworker is named twice in the model as one of the makers of horse equipment who does not have the knowledge the user has.

elements.context: ὁ μὲν ποιητὴς πίστιν ὀρθὴν ἕξει

signals.observation: πίστις and πιστεύω occur in stating that the maker will have correct belief and will make in trust, distinguishing belief from the knowledge possessed by the user.

elements.context: ἢ δόξαν ὀρθὴν διὰ τὸ ἐξ ἀνάγκης συνεῖναι τῷ εἰδότι
οὔτε ἄρα εἴσεται οὔτε ὀρθὰ δοξάσει ὁ μιμητὴς

signals.observation: δόξα and δοξάζω appear in the question about whether the imitator will have correct opinion, which is then denied.

elements.context: περὶ τῶν αὐλῶν, οἳ ἂν ὑπηρετῶσιν ἐν τῷ αὐλεῖν
οἳ ἂν ὑπηρετῶσιν ἐν τῷ αὐλεῖν

signals.observation: The aulos-player, aulos-maker, and auloi form a cluster illustrating the relationship between user and maker, with the user reporting which flutes serve well in playing.
ἐξαγγέλλω appears twice, stating that the user reports to the maker about good and bad qualities.

elements.context: εἴτε καλὰ καὶ ὀρθὰ εἴτε μή
περὶ ὧν ἂν μιμῆται πρὸς κάλλος ἢ πονηρίαν

signals.observation: Contrasting pairs recur: χρηστός and πονηρός, κάλλος and πονηρία, καλός and ὀρθός, repeatedly marking the evaluative dimension the user knows and the imitator does not.

elements.context: ἐπεὶ γυμνωθέντα γε τῶν τῆς μουσικῆς χρωμάτων

signals.observation: The poets' words are said to be stripped of the colors of music, revealing what they look like by themselves.

elements.context: ἐκ τῶν χρωμάτων δὲ καὶ σχημάτων θεωροῦσιν
γυμνωθέντα γε τῶν τῆς μουσικῆς χρωμάτων

signals.observation: χρῶμα recurs: the poet colors each of the crafts with words, viewers judge from colors and shapes, and the colors of music can be stripped away to reveal what the poets' words truly are.
The poets' words stripped of musical coloring are compared to beautiful faces that are no longer beautiful when they have left behind their bloom.

elements.context: οὕτω φύσει αὐτὰ ταῦτα μεγάλην τινὰ κήλησιν ἔχειν

signals.observation: Meter, rhythm, and harmony are said by nature to have a certain great enchantment.

elements.context: ἀλλʼ εἶναι παιδιάν τινα καὶ οὐ σπουδὴν τὴν μίμησιν

signals.observation: Imitation is said to be a certain play and not a serious thing.

elements.context: εἶναι παιδιάν τινα καὶ οὐ σπουδὴν τὴν μίμησιν

signals.observation: παιδιά and σπουδή are set in contrast, with imitation assigned to the former and denied the latter.

elements.context: τούς τε τῆς τραγικῆς ποιήσεως ἁπτομένους ἐν ἰαμβείοις καὶ ἐν ἔπεσι

signals.observation: Those who take up tragic poetry are said to work in iambics and in epic verses, named as the two poetic forms.
